candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest classifies this binary as malware with probability 0.94, and all 20 top SHAP features push toward cryptojacking (+0.005 to +0.009 each), so no feature argues against it. The strongest signal is a cluster of rotate-centric n-grams: ADD ROR (+0.009204), MOVZX ROL (+0.007770), MOV ROL (+0.007230, the most frequent at 0.004279), ROL ADD (+0.006877), ROL ROR (+0.005425) and ROR ROL (+0.005068). Dense rotate/add/move sequences are typical of hash and cipher round functions, the kind of work used in proof-of-work mining. A second cluster is carry-chain and multi-word arithmetic: SUB ADC (+0.007994), MOV ADC (+0.006545), ADD ADC (+0.005128), SUB SBB (+0.005266), SBB INC (+0.006240) and MOV SHRD (+0.005048). This pattern fits wide-integer or big-number arithmetic. A third cluster is generic glue and control flow (MOVZX PUSH, POP PUSH, SUB PUSH, CMP PUSH, CALL PUSH, CMP JNZ, CDQ MOV, ADD OR), which suggests byte-level data handling and loop or call structure around the compute kernels. Together these give a consistent profile of bit-rotation-heavy and carry-propagating arithmetic. The evidence has limits: it contains only mnemonic n-grams with low individual frequencies (0.000158 to 0.004279), and no function-level locations or API/string indicators were provided. The same instruction patterns also appear in legitimate cryptographic or compression code, so the assessment rests mainly on the model's high probability and the breadth of agreeing features rather than on any single definitive indicator.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Top feature. Add followed by rotate-right is a common building block of hash and cipher rounds and is consistent with mining-style hashing.
Zero-extended byte loads followed by a push suggest byte-wise data handling. Weak on its own, but it supports a data-processing routine.
Register save/restore glue. Low frequency, and it carries little meaning alone, but the model associates it with the malware class.
Subtract followed by add-with-carry indicates multi-word arithmetic, as in big-integer or wide-integer math.
Byte extraction directly followed by a rotate is typical of byte-oriented mixing in hash and cipher code.
Very rare (0.000158) but strongly weighted. Likely stack or argument setup around a compute routine; weak semantically.
Comparison followed by a push. Generic control-flow glue that the model links to the malware class.
Most frequent top-20 n-gram (0.004279). Loading a value and rotating it is characteristic of repeated round operations in hashing.
Rotate then add is the classic ARX (add-rotate-xor) pattern, supporting hash-like computation.
Sign extension before a move indicates signed 32/64-bit arithmetic handling. Low frequency, with modest interpretive value.
Add-with-carry after a move reinforces the carry-propagation, multi-precision arithmetic signal.
Arithmetic combined with bitwise OR, consistent with bit-mixing and combining operations in compute loops.
Subtract-with-borrow followed by an increment is another carry/borrow-chain pattern from wide arithmetic.
Call/argument-passing structure. Generic, but it contributes to the overall profile.
Compare-and-branch loop or condition idiom. Common in all code, so it is weak alone, though it is consistent with iterative compute loops.
Alternating left and right rotates are unusual in ordinary application code and typical of cryptographic mixing.
Subtract/borrow chain used for multi-word subtraction. Fairly frequent (0.002377), supporting the big-number arithmetic hypothesis.
Add followed by add-with-carry is the standard multi-word addition idiom, in line with wide-integer math.
Mirror of ROL ROR. Together the two reinforce a cluster of rotate-heavy code consistent with hash/cipher primitives.
Double-precision shift is used for 64-bit or wide shifts on 32-bit targets, in multi-word arithmetic and some crypto routines.
